content:
Hi everyone!
We released the preprint of our work Agentic Proving for Program Verification, co-authored with @Bas Spitters and Akhil Arora at Aarhus University, accessible at arXiv:2605.23772

Drawing from previous experiments of ours comparing various proof automation strategies on program verification tasks from the CLEVER and VERINA vericoding benchmarks in Lean, we investigated the best-performing strategy on the full program generation and verification pipeline of CLEVER, testing an agentic setup based on Claude Code.

We find that this setup is able to produce both high-quality specifications/implementations/proofs, and accurate feedback from the agent on its own attempts (as confirmed under manual human review), that proved able to identify underlying causes of failure and lingering bugs in the dataset. The solutions and feedback by the agents further highlighted some methodological limitations of isomorphism-against-a-ground-truth as an evaluation method for autoformalization of specifications, and displayed a performance close to saturation on the non-problematic portion of the datasets, pointing to the need for harder benchmarks leveraging bug-resilient evaluation methodologies.

We'd be grateful for any feedback on our work!
[ Please move this thread to a more appropriate channel if needed :) ]
This topic was moved here from #General announcements > Preprint: Agentic Proving for Program Verification by Patrick Massot.

Interesting works, thanks. Some questions:

"In all cases, a single attempt (pass@1) was made"

Looking at appendix C.2 was helpful. Being that the paper is suggesting harder benchmarks, what metrics do you think are useful other than just success? To me, it is very difficult to interpret the meaning of pass@n for a system that is already agentic like Claude and may make multiple attempts internally.

"The central challenge in autoformalizing NL sources is that of formalizing the intent behind them"

I agree. Your hand verification of this metric is a very insightful part of this paper, and your "alternatives to isomorphism based scoring" are interesting. Supposing a benchmark with precise NL specifications, and property based testing, do you see any issues with a system optimizing for these generalizing to real problems? I cloud see a model/system being encouraged to find the loosest formal spec possible that meets the properties and NL requirements, but maybe that isn't want we want (ignoring the separate problem of identifying intent).

I am interested to know your thoughts, or if these questions are malformed.

Hi @Connor Olson, I'll try to answer your questions :)

Being that the paper is suggesting harder benchmarks, what metrics do you think are useful other than just success?

In my mind, success is a metric intrinsic to the concept of benchmarking (i.e. how many tests a particular system passes), so no way of getting around that. The question is instead "what counts as a pass/success?", or in other words the evaluation method. Here we argue that evaluating specs proving that they are isomorphic to a ground-truth has limitations, as it often discards perfectly valid yet different interpretations of the same NL spec. There's no definitive answer to what would be the right alternative to this, but some candidate elements we identified like LLM feedback could contribute (not exclusively!) to such an alternative.

To me, it is very difficult to interpret the meaning of pass@n for a system that is already agentic like Claude and may make multiple attempts internally.

Yes, the interpretation of pass@n is not clear cut in the 'new' context of agentic systems (as also discussed in this message by @Jason Rute). Here we used pass@1 to signify that we did only one, totally independent run of the agent, simply meant as a clarification of "single attempt". Both the mentioned unclarity of pass@n in this context, and it not being meaningful (as n=1 was enough to achieve a high pass rate), led us not to use it as an evaluation metric.

Supposing a benchmark with precise NL specifications, and property based testing, do you see any issues with a system optimizing for these generalizing to real problems?

Yes and no. I guess that as with any optimization procedure of this kind, the risk of the system overfitting to the benchmark task and evaluation system is very real. But this may not be too problematic if the PBT is thorough enough, as that may be enough to force the system to generate "high-quality" solutions rather than "cheating" ones. Essentially, my trust in a system that is able to generate successful solutions with very strict PBT would be proportional to the strictness of the PBT itself . So, the answer to your question probably is "it depends on how much you would trust (a similar level of) PBT in a real world scenario" :)
